name: Own links
highlights: Your links page now shows only the places you list in your site's settings, and its latest-release button opens the release your home page features. A platform you have not added, or a section your site does not run, is left out instead of showing an empty link.
The music page's Listen button opens your own first listening platform, and the members' Vault sample drop no longer carries a sample streaming link.
Your site's privacy notice describes the newsletter as news and updates from your site, in plain words that fit any site.

2.8.17: Your site's front page can now be a page designed for you alone: when your own code (src/custom/pages.tsx) offers a front page, the site shows it in place of the composed or standard home, inside your usual header and footer.
A site built as a preview (TZOHAR_PREVIEW=1) now asks search engines to leave it out, in its page tags and headers, and its robots file names no sitemap, so you can share it by link before launch.
A site with no mailing list can drop the newsletter sign-up from its footer (layout.footerNewsletter set to false).
2.8.16: Image uploads in your site's admin now go into the folder set for your site, never one guessed from the site's name that another site could share. Tzohar Studio sets that folder for you when it sets up your admin or changes its password.
If the folder is not set, the admin says so in plain words and points to your site's support address instead of offering an upload that fails. Private Vault links need only your Cloudinary keys.
2.8.15: Your Vault and members' gallery can now ask Ebenworks Accounts about a visitor with a key of their own, so a busy day on your site no longer runs into the limit shared by everything on your server's address. Ebenworks gives you the key when you turn the Vault or a gated gallery on: set it as HUB_SESSION_INFO_KEY on your site's server only, never as a NEXT_PUBLIC_ setting. Without it nothing changes.

If that key is ever wrong or out of date, your site's server log says so (never the key itself) and the site leaves the key out for five minutes at a time, so your members still see their content while the key is fixed.
The live preview now takes drafts only from Tzohar Studio framing the page; opening the site elsewhere with the preview parameter shows the published site.

Your music pages' Spotify lookups now answer only for the artists and releases your site itself names, keep a cache of fixed size and age, and stop any one visitor's connection after 30 Spotify lookups an hour, so nobody can use your site as a free Spotify service and push it into Spotify's limits. When Spotify is busy or asks the site to slow down, the site waits before asking it again.
2.8.14: Your contact, newsletter and Inner Circle forms can no longer be used to mail strangers again and again. Every visitor's connection, every email address and the site as a whole have a daily limit on the mail the forms send, and the contact form now accepts only its own fields, each at a sensible length.

Newsletter and Inner Circle sign-ups now get a short email asking the person to confirm their address. The welcome, the note to you and (for the Inner Circle) the mailing-list add follow only when they press Confirm, so nobody can be signed up by someone else.

For limits that hold across all of your site's servers, add a Redis store: UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL and UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_TOKEN (Upstash, or Vercel's Redis integration). Without one each server counts on its own. MAIL_DAILY_CAP sets how many acknowledgements and confirm emails the forms send a day (60 if unset).

In your site's admin, changing CRM_PASSWORD now also ends the "signed in here before" status that lets a known browser past a site-wide sign-in pause, and that status can no longer be replayed from many addresses to keep guessing.

Breaking: A newsletter or Inner Circle sign-up is complete only when the person presses Confirm in the email they receive; the form now says "Check your inbox". The note telling you about a new subscriber arrives at that moment, not at sign-up.
2.8.13: When a save, upload or checkout on your site fails, visitors and editors now see a short plain message, and the technical detail behind it (which can name your site's code repository) stays in your site's server log. A content mistake in the admin still says which field to fix, and a missing setting is named.
Your site's checkout and fan profile now pass only the fan's Ebenworks Accounts sign-in to our service, never your site's other cookies such as the admin session or analytics.

A newsletter or Inner Circle signup now reports a failure when the note to you could not be sent, instead of saying it worked, and the welcome goes to the fan only once the note to you has gone. The example settings file no longer lists the old Stripe settings, which nothing reads.
2.8.12: Members-only content is checked on the server. While it builds the Vault and the gallery, the site asks Ebenworks Accounts whether the visitor holds a paid plan, and a non-member's page carries only what the free tier shows: an insider drop appears as its type, its date and "An Inner Circle drop", and the gallery shows the photo count over a blurred preview. Members see everything, as before.

A paid download can live in private storage. Give a Vault drop a `file` (a private Cloudinary asset on your site's own account) and members get a download link that stops working after ten minutes; non-members never get the address.
A visitor on the Free plan is no longer counted as a member anywhere on the site.

Photos that only the members' gallery shows are left out of the image lists every page sends to the browser. Photos kept in public/ can still be opened by anyone who has the exact address; sell files through the Vault's private `file` instead.

Breaking: Members see the Vault and the gallery only where the site runs on an ebenworks.co address, because the members check now runs on the site's server and only those addresses receive the Ebenworks Accounts sign-in. Checkout already needed this. On any other address every visitor sees the free tier.
2.8.11: Your site's admin (/admin) is harder to get into without the password. Every admin page now checks that you are signed in on its own, instead of relying on the frame around it, and every save, upload, sign-in and sign-out is accepted only from your site's own address, so a page somewhere else cannot make a signed-in browser change your site.

Sign-in is stricter. Five wrong passwords from one address within 15 minutes pause sign-in from there for 15 minutes, a burst of wrong passwords from many addresses pauses it for everyone except browsers that have signed in before, changing CRM_PASSWORD signs everyone out at once, and the session cookie is Secure and kept to your site alone in every setup.

Breaking: everyone signed in to the admin is signed out once when the site takes this release, because the session cookie has a new name; sign in again as usual. The admin needs https (or localhost when you work locally), and a link to /admin opened from another site asks for the password again.
Breaking: Everyone signed in to the admin is signed out once (the session cookie is renamed), and the admin needs https or localhost.
2.8.7: Images you upload in your site's admin (Media, Add an image) are stored on Cloudinary now, which resizes and converts them as it serves them, instead of being committed into your site's code. The repository stops growing with every photograph, and an upload no longer triggers a rebuild. The Media page lists your uploads with the address to copy; anything uploaded before keeps working and is listed under Earlier uploads.

Uploading needs three settings on the site: CLOUDINARY_CLOUD_NAME, CLOUDINARY_API_KEY and CLOUDINARY_API_SECRET (see .env.example). Without them the site builds and runs as before, and the upload asks for an image address instead.

Images uploaded in Tzohar Studio load from res.cloudinary.com. The site's image settings allow that address for Tzohar's own account only, in place of the shared Vercel Blob host, which any Blob store on the platform could use.
Breaking: The admin's image upload no longer writes into the repository. Until the three Cloudinary settings are added, it answers that upload is not set up and asks for an image address.
2.8.6: The three mails a client site sends to its visitors (the fan-club welcome, the newsletter welcome and the contact-form reply) open on a light header now: neutral grey with ink type and a blue top rule, where they used to open on a near-black or deep navy band. The body, the button and the footer are unchanged, and nothing about who receives what has moved.
2.8.5: A site that sets no colour mode now opens light, on every device. Until this release an absent `appearance.mode` meant "system", so the same site opened dark for any visitor whose phone or laptop was set to dark, and the first thing a new client saw of their own site depended on someone else's settings. The default is light everywhere now: the pre-paint script, the theme provider, the 404 page and Studio's live preview all read an absent mode as light.

Dark and System are still there, and both are a choice rather than an accident. Studio's Appearance panel lists Light first and shows it as the default; Dark opens on the dark palette, and System follows the visitor's OS exactly as before. A site that already set `mode` to anything keeps it.
2.8.4: 2.8.3 shipped two title helpers and the wrong one was easy to reach. `exactTitle()` used a hand-written title verbatim, which was right for "About <site>" and wrong for "Media": a client typing a short page name into an SEO field has not decided the site name should be absent, only that it should not appear twice. There is one function now. `fitTitle` leaves a title that already names the site alone, appends the name when the pair fits, and drops the name rather than letting it fall off the end when it does not. Every call site went through it, `exactTitle` is gone, and no page's title depends on how long the site's name happens to be.

An absolute title on a LAYOUT removes the `%s | <site>` template for everything beneath it, which is a Next behaviour worth knowing before you reach for `absolute`. Fixing the module layouts therefore stripped the site name from the release pages under `music/`, so a track rendered as a bare "Washa!". Those go through the fitter too. If you add an absolute title to a layout, check what its children render.

Nineteen meta descriptions were never clamped, so 2.8.2's slot fix had only ever covered three pages. Every metadata description in the engine goes through `clampDescription` now; it returns a short string unchanged, so it closes the class rather than the instances a measurement happened to surface. /ai's was rewritten to 153 characters rather than cut, since it is the engine's own copy.

Nine files that had improved in a client repo are back in the engine, which is what stops the same twelve conflicts recurring on every release. A nav group whose parent owns a page is a real link with its own disclosure button beside it, rather than one button whose only route to the page was a duplicate "overview" row; a pillar card takes an href and stretches the anchor over the whole card; a single image can run full width beneath the copy; a film can flip to the right; a link block can save a PDF instead of opening it; and the footer's categorised sitemap can be switched off. Each has its optional schema field, so nothing changes for a site that does not set one.

Two divergences are deliberate and stay. A client that removed every remote image host keeps its own `next.config.ts`: four of the five hosts here are needed by modules that load API images through `next/image`, so the engine cannot adopt an empty list. And `package.json` is merged rather than copied, which is why a client's own name and scripts survive a sync.
Measured on the reference build, 321 pages across five locales: zero doubled brands, zero descriptions over 158, and the only title over 60 is one release whose actual name is 67 characters long.
2.8.3: The title fitter no longer has the brand put back on the end of it. 2.8.2 dropped the site name from a title that would not fit the search slot; the locale layout declares `title.template = "%s | <site>"`, and Next applies that to any page setting a plain string — so the name came straight back, one separator later. Measured on the first client's live build: a 68-character post title rendered at 78, and every page whose own SEO title already ended in the site name rendered it twice, "About <site> | <site>". `fitTitle` returns `{ absolute }` now, which is the one form a parent template cannot reach, so the fix does not depend on each call site remembering.

Twenty-two routes were doubling the brand the same way and are fixed with it. Each of account, ai, biography, engagements, gallery, innovation (three routes), join, label artist, merch, music, posts index, press, research, tour and vault built its own "Title — <site>" and then had " | <site>" appended; /about did it in every locale, because the `metadata.aboutTitle` message a client writes already names them. A hand-written title — that message, or a composed page's `seo.title` — is now used exactly as typed, through `exactTitle()`: whoever wrote it has already decided whether the site name belongs in it. The four plain-label titles that do want the name (contact, links, privacy, macro-influencer) go through the fitter instead, so a client with a longer name cannot push one over the slot the way `macro-influencer` already did at 61.

Nineteen meta descriptions were never clamped, so the slot fix only ever covered three pages. Every metadata description in the engine now goes through `clampDescription`, which returns a short string unchanged — so it costs nothing where it was already fine and closes the class rather than the two instances that happened to show up in a measurement. /ai's was rewritten to 153 characters rather than cut, since it is the engine's own copy. Measured on the reference build afterwards: 321 pages, zero descriptions over 158, zero doubled brands, and the only five titles over 60 are one release whose actual name is 67 characters long.

Nine files that had improved in a client repo are back in the engine, which is what stops the same twelve conflicts recurring on every release. A nav group whose parent owns a page is a real link with its own disclosure button beside it, rather than one button whose only route to the page was a duplicate "overview" row; a pillar card takes an href and stretches the anchor over the whole card; a single image can run full width beneath the copy; a film can flip to the right; a link block can save a PDF instead of opening it; and the footer's categorised sitemap can be switched off on a site whose whole IA is five tabs. Each has its optional schema field, so nothing changes for a site that does not set one.

Two divergences are deliberate and stay. A client that removed every remote image host keeps its own `next.config.ts`: four of the five hosts here are needed by modules that load images from an API through `next/image`, so the engine cannot adopt an empty list. And `package.json` is merged rather than copied, which is why a client's own name and scripts survive a sync.
2.8.2: Your page titles and descriptions now fit the search result. Google shows about 60 characters of a title and 155 of a description and cuts the rest; nothing in the engine measured either, so how much of your snippet survived depended on how long you happened to write. Measured on a live client build: a 237-character site description on the home page, three post titles between 73 and 87 characters, and their excerpts between 183 and 193 — the tail of every one of them invisible in search, and on the long titles the subject sat right at the cut.

A title that will not fit drops the site name rather than letting it fall off the end, and a title longer than the whole budget on its own is handed over untouched — the browser cuts on pixel width and does it better than a character count, and an ellipsis stamped at 60 characters is worse than the browser's own. A description is cut at the last full sentence that still fits, and only falls back to a word boundary; it never cuts mid-word. Nothing you have written is rewritten, and nothing changes on the page itself.

This applies wherever the length is decided by your content: the site description, a composed page's title and description, and a post's title and excerpt. A page that sets its own SEO title or description in Studio is left exactly as written. Social cards keep the full line, because a card is not cut at 155 characters.
2.6.5: The contact page states where you are from your CONFIG, not from a message key named after somebody else's city. `location.based` was already published and already rendered two rows below for `from`; the "Based in" line printed `t("seoulKorea")` instead, which is "City, Country" in every trimmed build. A page whose whole job is to say where you are was saying City, Country while the config next to it said Seoul, South Korea. The message remains the fallback for a build that sets neither.
2.6.1: Next.js 16.1.6 → 16.2.12, which closes 28 published advisories. Two of them are the reason this is a release rather than a chore: a Middleware / Proxy bypass in App Router applications, and server-side request forgery through Server Actions and rewrites. This engine puts real properties in middleware — the CSP that decides who may frame a site, and on the control-plane side an auth gate that must fail closed and a host rewrite that must be unconditional — so a bypass class of bug is not theoretical here. Verified after upgrading: the frame-ancestors header still ships, and the control plane is still unreachable from the public hosts.

next-intl 4.8.3 → 4.13.4, closing an open redirect and a prototype pollution. The declared range already allowed the fix; only the lockfile was behind, which is the quiet way a patched advisory stays unpatched.

postcss and sharp are pinned by override. Next bundles its own copies (postcss 8.4.31, sharp 0.34.5) beneath the versions it resolves at the top level, so upgrading the direct dependency left the vulnerable copy in place — the tree had postcss twice, one patched and one not. Both are now single, patched copies in the engine and in Studio.

ESLint was walking generated build output. A bare `.next/**` ignore anchors at the repo root in flat config, so a nested `.next` was linted: ~9000 problems from 153 generated files, burying the ~40 real ones. The ignores are `**/`-prefixed now. This surfaces nine pre-existing react-hooks errors in engine components that nothing had been reporting, because `next build` on Turbopack does not run ESLint.

scripts/vercel-quota.mjs moved to scripts/private/, which is excluded from the sync. It reads OUR Vercel account's deployment allowance and was engine-classified, so it was queued to land in every client repo on their next sync — no credentials in it, but our fleet tooling is not part of a client's website. No client has it today, so nothing needs deleting.
2.6.0: Four more modules stop being the reference build. Enabling label, merch, press or influence used to give a client somebody else's brand — his record label's name, website and four social accounts; his merch photos; his press bio, fact sheet and logo downloads; his Instagram feed and thirty-one partner logos. All of it is content now (roster.json gains a label object; merch.json, press.json and influencer.json are new), and every section renders only when this site has something to put in it.

Two payment and account bugs, both the same shape. /api/checkout hardcoded the reference build's hub product key, so a client whose membership.ts named their own product still resolved prices from another site's PriceTable — a real payment for the wrong thing. /api/account/profile did it for the hub's per-product store, reading and writing one site's visitor profiles under another site's key. Both now read the client's own key and refuse to run without it.

The structured data a client publishes is theirs. The MusicGroup listed four albums and three tracks as literals and the label Organization was written out in full, so search engines were told a client's site was about another artist's discography and another company's record label. Both are built from content, and both are omitted entirely when there is nothing to describe — a wrong machine-readable claim is worse than none.

Module pages read their photographs from content. Five hero images, the AI portrait, the tour posters, the links avatar and the merch previews all pointed into a public/ path that only exists in the reference build's repo, so a client enabling a module got a 404 where the page's first impression should be.

src/data/instagram.ts is no longer 404 lines of one person's feed. It survived the 2.5.0 sweep because the music page imports it too, which made it look structural; the posts are content and the file is now just the selectors.

The engine ships no client's name. A whole-tree audit of engine-owned files went from 46 files and 180 lines naming another build to zero — including the release codename, which had been a client's actual first name.
2.5.0: The last per-site data left engine code. src/data/artist.ts was a 500-line TypeScript literal holding one artist's discography, government roles, brand partnerships and academic CV — part of the FRAMEWORK, so any client running the music/ai/links/influencer modules inherited someone else's career. It is content now (artist.json + a validated loader), and 174 of those lines turned out to be exports nothing imported at all.

Enabling a module later no longer breaks the build. A module's loader is engine code that imports client-owned JSON, so switching a module on used to add the loader and nothing else. The sync now seeds the missing starter content in the same commit — from the TEMPLATE, not from this release, because the engine repo doubles as the reference build and its content is one particular site's.

The music/ai/influencer pages tolerate absent data: a track with no album, an experience entry with no logo, a skill with an unknown icon. They previously assumed every field the reference build happened to fill in.
2.4.1: Our own documents stop shipping to clients. CLAUDE.md (this framework plus fleet-wide operational context) and PRODUCTIZATION.md (the business model and price list) were seeded into every client repo by the template. An internal pricing document in a customer repository should not be possible; both are excluded now.
2.4.0: The default home page is content, not code. It hardcoded the reference build's headline numbers, partner logos, three role panels, a featured post and a latest release — so every client shipped a home page advertising another artist, behind links to modules they had switched off and image paths that 404 in a client repo. It now reads src/data/home.json and skips whatever is absent; {} is a valid home, which is the right shape for a site that composes its own with the pages module.
Role panels only render when the module they link into is enabled. Three panels pointing at 404s was the previous behaviour on every client build.

The MusicGroup and label Organization schemas moved out of the root layout onto their own modules' pages. Emitting them sitewide claimed every page was about a music group, and it pinned one artist's discography into a core file that shipped to every client.
The label roster is content (src/data/roster.json + a validated loader), so one label's artists are no longer part of the engine.

src/config/membership.ts is client-owned. It is documented as a per-client file but was classified engine, so every client inherited a membership gate pointed at the reference build's product on the accounts hub — and src/lib/membership.ts no longer falls back to that product key, because a wrong-but-plausible answer from the hub is worse than failing closed.
2.3.1: The reference build's personal artefacts (Wikipedia draft, Wikidata sync scripts) moved to scripts/private/ and are now EXCLUDED from the sync. They were 57 mentions of another person's name in every client repo, engine-adjacent only by accident of living under scripts/.
The remaining build scripts no longer hardcode the reference build in default paths, logo filenames or DOM selectors.
2.3.0: A client repo now only carries code for the modules it enables. requireModule() already 404s a disabled module's routes, which is enough for a visitor and nothing else: the FILES still shipped, so every client repo contained the reference build's music pages, its record-label roster, its Instagram data and its press quotes — dead weight in their build and another brand's copy in their repo. The sync no longer offers a disabled module's files, and offers the ones already present for removal.

Ownership is derived, not hand-listed: requireModule() calls give the gated subtree, imports are followed forward, and a file is prunable only when EVERY module that can reach it is disabled and no core entrypoint reaches it. Generated into packages/schema/src/module-paths.ts by `npm run module-paths`; a file the table doesn't know about is never pruned.

Measured on the first real client (crm + pages + posts): 70 files removed and the build goes from 351 prerendered pages to 45. Reversible — turning a module back on makes the next sync restore its files.
2.2.1: The light hero wash no longer erases the subject on a phone. Its top band was 72% paper over 190px — doing the navbar's job over exactly the 120–180px where a head lands on a narrow frame — so a hero cropped to show a face showed a rumour of one. Now 58% over 120px, which still carries dark ink over a bright plate.
2.2.0: Mobile is tighter. The band-padding FLOOR governs every viewport up to ~933px, so a floor of 3.5rem meant every section on a phone was separated by 112px of nothing; the hero is shorter and its bottom padding smaller now that the fact row is hidden. Desktop is bit-identical — above 933px the vw term wins either way.

The web app manifest is generated from config (src/app/manifest.ts) instead of being a static file copied into every client's public/. It was never replaced after copying, so the first real client's live site offered to install as an app named after the reference build, with a music-producer description, on their own domain.

favicon.ico moved out of src/app/ (engine-owned) into public/ (client-owned). Next serves the app-dir icon with precedence, so the sync had been shipping the reference build's favicon into every client repo and overriding theirs — verified by md5: the first client's live favicon was byte-identical to ours.

Fourteen route layouts stopped hardcoding the reference build's domain in their canonical + hreflang tags. A canonical is an instruction to index the OTHER url, so this was pointing clients' SEO at somebody else's site; the language map was also fixed at five locales, advertising alternates that 404 for an en-only build. Both now come from site.url and site.locales via routeAlternates().
The schema.org graph no longer carries hardcoded reference-build URLs in @id, url and publisher fields.
2.1.3: schema.org `nationality` now emits a country. `location.from` is written for humans ("Mwenezi, Zimbabwe"), and the whole string was being published as a Country name — so the structured data search engines read declared a Country named after a rural district.

Core-route photo heroes (contact, about) now follow the theme instead of forcing a dark band onto a light page. A light-theme site was opening its contact page on a near-black slab with a light-ink navbar over it — the same defect composed-page heroes had before they gained a light plate, on the routes nobody re-checked. Name a bright frame in Brand → "Page hero photo — light mode".

The light hero wash is rebalanced. At 97% paper it was legible but the photograph was gone; it now sits at a tested middle where the image reads as colour and place and dark ink keeps a comfortable margin. All four scrims (light/dark × wide/narrow) live in one shared module, because these numbers had already been wrong twice in two components.

A hero's fact row (Based in / Field / Affiliation) is hidden below the sm breakpoint. On a phone it became ~200px of stacked label/value pairs that pushed the affiliations marquee — the thing that establishes credibility at a glance — entirely below the fold. Still in the DOM for crawlers and screen readers, still on desktop.
Pillar cards take an optional photograph, so the set where a reader decides which domain is theirs isn't three blocks of text.

The footer credits the build ("A Tzohar site — built by Ebenworks & Statotech") and no longer prints the subject's birthplace as if it were an address; that fact still feeds the about page and the schema.org Person.
2.1.1: Light-mode heroes were unreadable on a phone: the narrow white wash mirrored the dark ramp's opacities, and the mobile crop was shared between two different photographs, putting a face directly behind the title.
New positionMobileLight so a light plate can be cropped for narrow screens on its own.
Studio can edit the whole background — the light-mode photo, its scrim and both crops.
2.1.0: Studio's preview is now this site itself, framed and fed your unsaved draft — same components, CSS, fonts and motion as production, because it is production rendering a draft. It replaced a miniature re-implementation that rendered 9 sections where a real page had 12.
Appearance changes (colour, font, paper, radius, mode) apply live with no reload, using the same CSS generator the server injects — so they look right rather than approximately right.
Selecting a section in Studio scrolls this site's preview to it and flashes it.
Real device viewports — 1440 / 1280 / 834 / 390 with rotate — sized in true CSS pixels so this site's own media queries decide the layout.
2.0.0: Five new page-section types: gallery (lightbox), video (poster + inline player), journey (annotated map/timeline), portfolio (printable one-pager), postList (filterable article index).
Posts — a dated, reverse-chronological writing surface with categories, drafts and a safe plain-text body, separate from composed pages.
A client-facing CMS at /admin: posts, page sections, media uploads and site settings, committed straight to the repo. No hub account, no dependency on Studio being up.
Heroes gained a light-mode plate, per-mode scrims and a mobile crop, so one hero block can be dark-cinematic and light-airy without duplicating it.
Navigation panels with icons, blurbs and a feature tile; card grids gained an index variant for small source images.
Every route's SEO, every transactional email and the schema.org Person now read from site config instead of carrying the previous client's copy.
Contact inquiry forms are chosen in config, and filtered to the ones this build has copy for, so a trimmed messages file can never break the page.
Contrast-corrected paper palettes — the noir preset's tonal ladder is separable in both modes, and ink-3 clears 4.6:1 on every band tone.
2.6.2: package.json is MERGED into a client repo now, not overwritten. It is the one engine-owned file that is genuinely shared — the engine decides which framework versions the code compiles against, the repo decides what it is called and what commands it offers — and copying it wholesale did two wrong things at once. It pushed our internal tooling into client repos (`npm run quota` reads OUR Vercel account's deployment allowance; `hooks:install` points at a .githooks/ directory a client does not have), and it destroyed any hand-trim, which is why the template's narrower scripts block kept coming undone. Dependencies, devDependencies and overrides are the engine's; name, version, licence and anything unrecognised stay the client's; keys only they have are kept, because dropping a dependency somebody added breaks their build.

Which scripts ship is DERIVED, not listed. A script is offered when every repo path it names is engine-classified — i.e. when the sync will actually put those files there. So `next build` ships (names no path), `node scripts/gen-module-paths.mjs` ships, and `scripts/private/vercel-quota.mjs` (ours) and `.githooks` (theirs to write) are both withheld for the same reason rather than by name. Add a script to the engine and the rule already knows the answer; there is no allowlist to forget.

package.json can no longer be reported as a conflict. Previously a client who added a single dependency saw it as one forever, because "differs from the release" was the only question being asked — the merge is now the resolution, and the recorded baseline is the sha of what was actually written rather than the release's, which would have been a lie about the bytes.

The template refresh merges it too, where it matters most: a fault in the template is one fault per future customer. It also warns when a repo has dependencies the engine does not — package-lock.json is still copied whole, and npm ci (what Vercel runs) fails outright on a lockfile that disagrees with its manifest.
2.6.3: A dark band on a themed site painted the WRONG accent. `.section-invert` is the engine's scoped dark island — the "dark hero on a light page" look — and it pinned the whole dark palette including `--color-ocean`, hardcoded to the base blue. Being a descendant rule, a preset's `.dark[data-theme="…"]` block could never reach inside it, so on emerald, rose, violet, sunset or slate EVERY inverted hero and CTA rendered the default blue while the rest of the page was the client's colour. Found on a live emerald build whose hero button was blue; each preset now declares the accent its island uses, and `default` is unchanged. A client's own custom accent still wins over their preset inside the island — that precedence is now covered by the specificity of the new rule rather than by luck.
2.6.4: The header knows a dark hero band from what is RENDERED, not from a config switch. `layout.heroTone: "dark"` is set by hand, and a composed page whose first block carries `tone: "invert"` is a dark band whether or not anyone remembered to set it — so in light mode the bar sat transparent over a near-black hero with its light-mode chrome: dark-ink logo on near-black, invisible, with the nav ink and the contact pill to match. It now reads the first child of <main> for `.section-invert`, which is exactly the question being asked, and inverts the whole bar. `.section-invert-auto` (a core route's photo hero, dark only in dark mode) is deliberately not matched, and the config switch still forces it on for a hero that is dark by art direction. Verified across all three: invert hero in light mode inverts and shows the light-plate logo; a light hero does not; /contact does not, in either mode.
2.7.0: `appearance.mode` finally does what it says. The pre-paint script honoured it and then ThemeProvider undid it: the provider initialised to light, read only localStorage and the OS setting, removed the `.dark` class the script had just added, and wrote "light" to localStorage on EVERY mount rather than on a toggle. So a site configured dark opened cream on a light-mode machine, and every visitor who has ever loaded any site on this engine is carrying a stored preference they never expressed. A pinned mode now outranks that stored value in the provider and in both copies of the inline script (the site and the 404 page), localStorage is written only by an explicit toggle, and the toggle itself is hidden where the mode is pinned — a control that cannot change anything is worse than no control. Verified with the storage still poisoned, on a light-mode OS: 18 mode x stored x OS combinations, no mismatches, and `system` behaves exactly as before.

Two permanently-dark plates stopped inverting. `bg-ink` is the INK colour — near-black in light mode, near-WHITE in dark — so using it to mean "a dark plate" flips to a white slab in dark mode and takes any literal `text-white` contents with it. The journey map, whose graticule, routes, pin labels and caption are all white, became a cream rectangle on a dark site; the photographic home hero flashed a white band behind white type on both breakpoints. Both are `.section-invert` now, which is what "dark regardless of the page" actually means. The `bg-ink text-bg` pills are a different thing and are untouched.

A page can be in the menu without taking a tab. `nav.inBar: false` keeps a composed page in the footer sitemap, the CRM listing and the mobile bar's logic while leaving the top-level tabs — previously the only way to shorten a seven-tab bar was to delete `nav`, which also removed the page from the footer and left it reachable by URL alone. Core entries gained the same choice through `layout.navHide` ("home", "about"), because a site composed entirely of pages was spending a tab to repeat the wordmark two inches to its left. Both are editable in Studio, and the CRM now says "a top tab" or "footer only" instead of calling both "in the menu".

`site.cta` gives the header one button that names what the site is asking for — "Partner with us", "Book the band" — and steps Contact down to a plain link beside it. Contact is a destination; the CTA is the ask, and a filled pill reading "Contact" spent the bar's only emphasis on the weaker of the two. The href may carry a hash, so it can land on one of the contact page's inquiry tabs rather than the generic form. Unset, the header is exactly as it was.

The composed-page blocks line up. A `wide` gallery tile made its row taller than an aspect-locked neighbour could fill, leaving a measured 309px of dead space inside one cell. Pillar cards bottom-aligned the tag BLOCK, which is not the same as aligning its label — cards whose chips wrapped differently started their label a chip-row apart (3104 / 3068 / 3068 px), so the tag band is now a shared row in the outer grid and every label sits on one line (3088 / 3088 / 3088). A portrait video stands ~260px taller than the copy beside it and banked all of it into one hole below the text; a single image beside prose did the same. Logo strips are an even N-column row with hairline dividers on desktop, where `flex-wrap` had been breaking seven logos into 5+2, and the marquee is kept below `lg` where seven cells would be 50px wide.

Display type stops breaking mid-word and mid-margin. A long hero title steps down a size, because headlines scale with LINE LENGTH and not just viewport width; `hyphens: none` keeps "socio-economic" whole, its hard hyphen having been read as a break opportunity in 67px type; the hero quote mark moved from inline to block so the copy column keeps one left margin instead of indenting its first line past everything beneath it; and stacked hero buttons match widths on a phone. Eyebrows balance their wrap, and the mobile tab bar shortens a label only when it cannot fit — taking the LAST word, so "Public Diplomacy" is "Diplomacy" and not "Public".

The generated portfolio PDF speaks in one voice: its one big headline was Times-Bold against a Helvetica document. Also fixed: the journey map's active pill put a mid-grey number on a near-white ground in dark mode, measured at 2.27:1 where 12px text needs 4.5:1.
2.8.0: The header keeps floating over the hero, and hero copy can no longer collide with it. `overHero` held the bar fully transparent for the first 60svh of scroll — but a hero's copy sits near the BOTTOM of an 84vh band, so it scrolled up underneath a bar that had no background yet and the two overlapped, on every composed page, in both modes, until you were past 60% of the viewport. The bar's surface is now its own layer so it can fade, and its opacity is driven by the hero copy's measured distance from the bar rather than by scroll distance. It is anchored to the gap AT REST, so the scrim is exactly 0 at the top of every page — the float is the look and it is kept — and reaches 1 the moment the copy would touch. Measured on 7 routes x light/dark x 1440/390: no state has copy at or under the bar without a full scrim, and no page carries a scrim at rest. Solidifying on the first scroll was tried first and rejected: it fixes the overlap by throwing the float away.

`appearance.toggle` separates the default palette from whether visitors get a switch. Until now those were one decision: `system` meant a toggle and followed the OS, while `light`/`dark` pinned the site and HID the control — so "open dark, but let people choose" was unexpressible, which is exactly what a dark-first client asked for. With a pinned mode plus `toggle: true`, the pinned mode is the first-visit default, the toggle is shown, and an explicit choice is remembered; unset, a pinned mode stays locked as before. The precedence lives in three places that must agree — ThemeProvider and the pre-paint script in both the site and the 404 page — and all three were changed together. Studio only offers it beside a pinned mode, and its old help text ("they can still toggle") was false under exactly the modes that hid the control.

`logoStrip` gains `mono`, for white knock-out partner marks. A supplied strip is normally white-on-transparent for a dark design; rendered unchanged on a light band it is white on cream, i.e. gone. The colour originals are no help — they ship as opaque JPEG/PNG and land as white boxes — so `mono` inverts the same marks to ink on a light band and leaves them white inside a dark one. Off by default: inverting a full-colour logo wrecks it.

A composed page's leading hero photograph gets `priority`. next/image lazy-loads by default, so the largest element on first paint arrived after the copy and the band showed empty dark for a beat — worst on a heavier frame, where a whole hero read as a rendering failure. Only the first hero opts in; preloading every section's backdrop would trade one late image for six.
2.8.1: A site downloads only the CJK webfonts its locales need. The three Noto families (KR/SC/JP) were declared unconditionally in the root layout, and `next/font` runs at COMPILE time — the call site alone fetches the family whether or not the result is used, which was measured both ways: 434 woff2 either way, 434 → 85 once the calls go. So an English-only client was spending 349 build-time requests to fonts.gstatic.com and 12.6 MB of its 14.4 MB font output on scripts it never serves, and no condition could have prevented it. The declarations moved into a GENERATED `src/lib/cjk-fonts.generated.ts` (scripts/gen-cjk-fonts.mjs, same generate-and-commit pattern as module-paths.ts), written from `locales.enabled`, regenerated by `prebuild`/`predev` so a deploy cannot ship a stale set, with `npm run cjk-fonts:check` for drift. A five-locale site is unchanged and still ships all three.

This was a build DEPENDENCY on Google, not just weight: a client deploy failed outright when a handful of those ~350 URLs 404'd against a restored Vercel build cache — on a site that serves no Japanese. Fewer families is fewer ways for someone else's CDN to fail your build.

`:lang(ko|zh|ja)` no longer falls back to Times New Roman. The rules read `var(--font-ko), var(--font-sans), system-ui` — which looks like a graceful stack and is not: an undefined custom property invalidates the whole declaration AT COMPUTED-VALUE TIME, so the rest never applies and the browser uses its own default. Latent while all three families were always declared; reachable the moment they became conditional, and measured as serif body text on a build shipping no KR family. Each var() now carries its own fallback plus real system CJK faces (Apple SD Gothic Neo / PingFang / Hiragino), so a site serving a CJK locale without the webfont gets a proper face. Same trap as `--font-sans` in the layout — this is the second time it has cost something.

The generated font module is classified as the CLIENT'S, not the engine's. It lives in `src/lib/` but is derived from the client's own `locales.enabled`, so an engine sync would have handed every client the reference build's three-family copy and silently undone the fix.
